title: Tooth Emoji 🦷 Meaning: Dentists, Sweet Tooths and Smiles
description: 🦷 stands for teeth, dentist visits, braces, a lost baby tooth or a sweet tooth. Learn how people use the tooth emoji in texts, captions and dental office posts.
summary: 🦷 is a single white molar with its roots showing. It stands for teeth and dental care: dentist appointments, braces, whitening, wisdom tooth removal and children losing baby teeth. It also gets used for a sweet tooth, for toothaches, and for the tooth fairy’s nighttime visits.
meaning: The tooth emoji is refreshingly literal. People reach for it when teeth are the subject: an upcoming cleaning, a cracked filling, new aligners, a whitening appointment. Dental practices put it in social posts and appointment reminders because it is instantly recognizable. Unlike many body-part emojis, it has no widespread slang meaning, so it rarely causes misunderstandings.

Childhood milestones give it some of its warmest uses. Parents share the news that a first baby tooth came in or fell out, often with 🧚 for the tooth fairy and 💰 for the coin left under the pillow. In those messages 🦷 is celebratory rather than clinical, a small badge of growing up that grandparents and aunts respond to with hearts.

Pain is the other common theme. Wisdom teeth, root canals and toothaches send people to their phones looking for sympathy, and 🦷 paired with 😭 says plenty on its own. After oral surgery, a swollen-cheek selfie captioned with 🦷 and an ice pack is a familiar post, usually followed by complaints about living on smoothies and soup.

The phrase “sweet tooth” lets the emoji stray from dentistry. 🦷🍭 or 🦷🍩 announces a craving for sugar, often with ironic awareness of what the dentist would say. Approved in 2018, it arrived late compared with eyes, ears and mouths, but it filled an obvious gap; until then, people talking about teeth had to make do with a grinning face.

contexts.label: At the dentist
contexts.body: Patients use 🦷 to complain, joke or brag about appointments: “no cavities 🦷✨.” Dental offices and orthodontists use it in posts about cleanings, whitening and braces, and in reminder texts. It reads as friendly and tidy in that setting, which helps explain why it shows up so often in dental marketing.

contexts.label: With kids
contexts.body: Losing a tooth is a big event for young children, and parents record it with 🦷 in family chats and captions. The tooth fairy, the gap-toothed grin and the coin under the pillow form a little cluster of emojis around it. Relatives tend to reply with hearts and questions about how much the tooth fairy pays these days.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: Outside dental news, 🦷 mostly appears in sweet tooth jokes or as quick shorthand for pain: “my tooth 🦷😩” is enough explanation for canceling plans. It also shows up when someone gets braces removed or finishes aligner treatment and wants to show off the result, usually with a big grinning face right beside it.

A sweet tooth, or a guilty craving for candy.
Toothache, dental surgery or dread before an appointment.
Clean, bright teeth after a cleaning or whitening.

confusedWith.difference: 🦴 is a bone, used for dogs, skeletons and anatomy jokes. Both are white, but 🦴 has knobbed ends and no crown or roots. If the topic is teeth or the dentist, the tooth is the right pick.
😬 shows clenched, bared teeth and means awkwardness or “yikes.” People sometimes use it for dental anxiety, but it is a face expressing tension, while 🦷 is the tooth itself with no emotion attached.

👄 shows lips and is linked to kissing, talking and sometimes flirting. 🦷 isolates the tooth and points to dental care. When the subject is teeth rather than lips or speech, the tooth is the clearer choice.

avoid: Do not use it as a cheerful reaction when someone describes serious dental pain or an emergency.
Avoid it as a stand-in for smiling, since readers will think of the dentist rather than happiness.
design: A single tooth, usually a molar, drawn in white or off-white with a rounded crown and two roots extending downward. Some designs add a soft highlight to suggest a clean, healthy tooth. The look is broadly consistent across platforms: a tidy cartoon tooth of the kind seen on dental office signs. It does not support skin tones.

faqs.a: Usually something about teeth: a dentist visit, braces, a toothache or a child losing a tooth. Next to candy or dessert, it means a sweet tooth. It has no common hidden slang meaning, so the literal reading is almost always the right one.

faqs.q: When was the tooth emoji added?
faqs.a: It was approved in 2018 as part of Emoji 11.0. Before then there was no dedicated way to show a tooth, and people improvised with grinning faces or the mouth emoji when talking about dentists or teeth.

faqs.q: What emojis go with a lost tooth?
faqs.a: A popular set is 🦷 with 🧚 for the tooth fairy, 💰 for the reward and 😁 for the gap-toothed grin. Parents often add 🎉 to mark the milestone. Together they tell the whole story in a single line.

faqs.q: Why do dentists use the tooth emoji?
faqs.a: It is the clearest symbol of their work and looks friendly rather than clinical. Practices use it in social posts, reminders and promotions for cleanings, whitening or orthodontics, where it signals the topic immediately without showing anything that might unsettle anxious patients.
